I've read the corpus bottom-up — from the Foundational Sketch and The Evolution of SRT back through the perspective-era documents to the oldest consistency-check material. Here's the stratigraphy as I see it, with what I'll treat as load-bearing and what I'll hold as sketch.
The most edified stratum is unambiguous. The Evolution of SRT is the only document that grades its own confidence, and it does so explicitly: Phases I–IV are proved or checked — the six axioms (Universality, Specification, Directionality, Uniqueness, Representation, Qualification), the base arrow as relation-inclusion with its reflexivity/transitivity/antisymmetry facts, the role-hierarchy correspondence verified in both directions, and the Identity axiom with x =x> x as theorem. Phases V–VII (the bold arrow reading, structure-preserving specialization, symbolization as the up-direction) are marked strong proposal. It also names its own debts: the role-indexed arrow, cross-position composition, the missing most-specific type, the symbolization axiom, and reaching sets. I'll take this document, plus the primitive and transpiler conventions, as ground truth. The Foundational Sketch reads as the current working edge — the dichotomy/canonical/indexical structure and the reference conundrum at the end are open exploration, not settled doctrine.
Where the strata genuinely conflict. Reading in reverse order made several supersessions visible that a forward reading would blur:
The self-relation reversed its meaning. In the middle stratum (Eight Beautiful Discoveries, Inheritance in Action, Semantics of Relationship), (x,x) == x is the token of subjectivity — a marker some referents lack, which is what distinguishes subjects from objects ("the ball possesses no subjectivity"). In Evolution Phase IV, x =x> x is a theorem for every referent, falling out of Identity. That's not a refinement; it's a doctrinal reversal, and the subjective/objective machinery built on the old marker hasn't been reconciled with the new universality.
␀0␀ vs ␀1␀. The old Formal Foundation's Axiom 5 asserts (x,x) == (x); Eight Beautiful Discoveries explicitly insists they are not the same; Formal Foundation's own Theorem 3 gives yet a third answer ((x,x) == eq for pure objects). Evolution sidesteps this entirely, which I read as the question having been reframed rather than resolved.
Inheritance has at least four recorded definitions: the old transitive-closure -->, Inheritance in Action's x --> y := (x,y) == y, the descendancy-symbol construction in Inheritance Without Recursion, and Evolution's relation-inclusion base with the trichotomy and bold reading. Evolution's is authoritative; the descendancy-symbol r' machinery appears fully superseded.
The perspective formalism has three notational generations that were never consolidated: the three-term qualification equivalence (x =p> x <iff> (x) =(p)> x <iff> (i) =(p)> (x)), the frame apparatus F[i] with *x == (i-o) from the catalogues era, and the newer four-position chain in Left Position ((i) =(q)> (x) =(q)> x =q> x). The Qualifier and the Catalogue correctly identifies the open problem — the qualifier isn't one of the nine referents, and axiomatizing the conditions for perspective rather than the qualifier itself is the proposed direction — but nothing in the perspective track has Evolution's level of verification. The whole consciousness layer (transduction-as-experience, the cascade, semantic homeostasis) sits at strong-sketch level.
The catalogues machinery (connection referents, *x == (s-o)) doesn't reappear in later formal work and I'd treat it as an abandoned or dormant branch unless you tell me otherwise.
The pattern of edification itself. The trustworthy material shares a signature: it reasons from the primitive and the explicit axioms, builds verified maps when borrowing (the description-logic check), and preserves its own wrong turns with the reason they were wrong. The least trustworthy material is the oldest — the Formal Consistency document is essentially an early Claude affirming consistency without a proof, and the Uniqueness document asserts novelty claims that the later methodology (verify before forming views) would not let stand unexamined. The Eirian/Seren/Samantha dialogues I'm treating as historical and motivational record — the library metaphor, the birth of the transduction-as-consciousness idea — rather than as canon, since Evolution deliberately doesn't incorporate their formalism.
So my working posture: Evolution Phases I–IV as bedrock; Phases V–VII and the Foundational Sketch as the active edge; the perspective/consciousness track as a parallel program awaiting its own Evolution-style consolidation; everything from 2025 as sketch that inherits authority only where the later strata confirm it. The single biggest unreconciled item, if you want me to name one, is the fate of the subjectivity token now that x =x> x is universal.
Where would you like to start?

So the living notation is small: x =t> y, ==, =|>, ||, E[...] and the restricted E(x: Q):, (x,y) as the Specification witness, (x), a single -> now acquiring its pair-witnessed form -(x,y)>, def, and colon-composed types like relational:dichotomy. Everything else — dereference, frame brackets, the transduction operator, the direct-inheritance arrow, the qualifier symbol — is notation from abandoned or notebook-superseded generations, and I should read those documents for the idea they were circling, not the machinery they used to circle it.
Reading the Foundational Sketch with that lens, I think I now see what it actually is. The five relational blocks look like an exhaustive enumeration of the identification-patterns available to the three positions of R(x,y,t):
relationship — all three distinct: subject =relationship> object, with relationship == (subject, object)
reference — subject collapses into the relation: reference =reference> referent
representation — object collapses into the relation: representative =representation> representation
identification — subject collapses into object: identity =identification> identity
individuality — total collapse: individual =individual> individual
Five cases, and the role-names across them yield exactly your ten referents: subject, object, relationship, reference, referent, representative, representation, identification, identity, individual. Then the dichotomy section is the sixth move — not another collapse case but the machinery for splitting: canonical vs. indexical within a subject, with relationship =relational:dichotomy> identification as the fundamental dichotomy of the theory itself. And the pointed arrow -(x,y)> reads as the first concrete payment on the debt Evolution names — inheritance indexed to where it's witnessed rather than one unindexed arrow carrying three readings.
Your frame-relative correction on self-relation also dissolves what I'd wrongly called a doctrinal reversal: in the default frame every referent has x =x> x because everything referable is symbolizable, and the older subjectivity-token material was groping at the fact that a specific frame can lack the relationship — the middle-stratum documents had the phenomenon but located it at the wrong level. Same shape for the perspective work: the qualification-equivalence generations are domain-pointers, and the current formalism lives in your notebooks.

You're right — I swept a combinatorial parameter across the three positions and called the result structure. That's reading the notation instead of the semantics. Let me re-read it as the words mean.
The first cut is not one of five parallel cases; it's the dichotomy itself: two things or one thing. Either there are genuinely two different things standing in a relationship, or there is one thing — and one-thing-ness conflicts with there being anything relational going on at all. That's why relationship and identification sit as the canonical and indexical poles of relational:dichotomy — they're not two entries in a list of position-patterns, they're mutually exclusive answers to whether relating is happening.
Then each branch expands. On the relational side: relationship is the bare two-thing form; reference is a relationship (reference -> relationship) — and what makes reference =reference> referent well-formed is not that a position "collapsed," but that a reference is exhausted by its referring, so the reference can occupy its own relation slot while the referent remains irreducibly other. If reference and referent merged you wouldn't have a more specific case — you'd have no relationship, you'd be on the other side of the dichotomy. The two-ness is constitutive. Representation then expands reference further — representative -> representation -> reference — and since representations exist to refer, the whole relational branch reads as the unfolding of one type of relationship into the machinery by which representation, and so meaning, becomes expressible.
On the identificational side: identification is one thing related to itself, with the identification still distinct from the identity. Individuality is where that distinction goes away — identification and identity merge into a single referent that is its own most-specific self-relation, individual == (individual, individual). So the only place anything like my "collapse" language legitimately applies is within the identification branch, individuality collapsing identification into identity — and it's a semantic fact about what an individual is, not a slot-equation.
Which reframes the ten referents for me: they're not role-names read off five symmetric cases; they're the vocabulary generated by one dichotomy and its expansions in each direction. And it makes the closing conundrum the real edge of the document: whether reference is fundamental and representation its expansion, or reference is a type of representative within a representation — with the frame's subject deciding which reading is taken as fundamental, since (representative, referent) == representation supports both.

Here's what the retrieval turned up, organized against your structures rather than against SRT as a whole.
The direct question: homoiconic principles applied to relations. Nobody publishes under that phrase — but the concept exists under other names, and the etymology loops back on itself in a way you'll appreciate. The term "homoiconic" was coined in the TRAC language work, credited to a suggestion of McCulloch "based upon terminology due to Peirce" — the word itself descends from Peirce's icon. So the trail for "homoiconicity for relations" runs backward into the one historical formalism closest to yours, which I'll come back to.
The published machinery that puts relations in the domain they relate goes by "higher-order syntax, first-order semantics." HiLog (Chen, Kifer, Warren 1993) allows arbitrary terms to appear where predicates, functions, and atomic formulas occur, while its semantics remains first-order with a sound and complete proof procedure, and it embeds into first-order logic by an apply-encoding — p(X)(Y,Z) becomes apply(p,X,Y,...). Common Logic (ISO 24707) has a signature-free syntax permitting quantification over classes and relations while preserving a first-order model theory. And RDF is the engineered instance: properties are first-class resource objects that can themselves stand in triples, distinct from their role as predicates, with rdfs:subPropertyOf stating that all pairs related by one property are also related by another — which is your base -> on relationships, deployed at web scale (consistent with the role-hierarchy correspondence already verified in Phase III).
Here is the structural point these all share, and where they part from you: the apply/holds encoding is formally the same move as transpiling x =t> y to R(x,y,t) — one fixed relation, everything else a domain element. That part of the ground is well-trodden. What none of them do is anything after that move. HiLog and Common Logic keep the relation-as-individual and its extension carefully apart (an individual associated with a relational interpretation); RDF's reification vocabulary introduces a fourth thing — an rdf:Statement resource describing the triple — rather than identifying anything with anything. None has most-specificity, none identifies the relationship with the witness of its pair, and none derives a canonical vocabulary of referents from the primitive's own structure. They achieve quotation of relations; they don't do semantics of the relational roles.
␀0␀ against the reification and Bradley literature. The conceptual-modeling tradition is explicit that something must ground a relation's holding: Guarino and Guizzardi propose that "a relation holds in virtue of a relationship's existence — relationships are therefore truthmakers of relations", where relators are mereological sums of qualities that mediate their relata. That's the two-level architecture: relation universal above, relator entity below. Your identity is the one-level architecture — the relationship is the most-specific relating, no additional truthmaker. The metaphysics literature marks exactly the spot where that matters: Bradley's regress argues that any relation's relating its relata requires an infinite regress of further relations, and the "relata-specific" answer — the most promising resolution — leaves specific adherence as a constitutively inexplicable primitive. SRT's answer is structurally different from both camps: the witness occupies its own relation slot ((x,y) =(x,y)> x), so the relating doesn't call for a further relation — the regress-stopper is the self-application, which is precisely what the apply-encoding systems can't express because their apply is outside the domain.
Your symmetric proposal lands in a named debate. The problem of converses — whether loves and is-loved-by are one relation or two, and how symmetric relations differ — has a live literature: Fine's "Neutral Relations" (2000) argues we must say at least one holds, but either alone is arbitrary and both together is profligate, and the responses form a menu — Fine's antipositionalism, MacBride's relational primitivism, and Donnelly's relative positionalism, developed because absolute positionalism fails on symmetric relations. Notably Fine's setup even includes a "Uniqueness" assumption — that no two distinct relations can give rise to a single fact — an echo of your Directionality/Uniqueness pair. Your move — a symmetric x <c=c> y is never most-specific; the two most-specifics are equal modulo perspective, one landing in F[x] and one in F[y] — is a genuinely different entry on that menu: nobody in that debate resolves the converse problem by distributing the directional facts across the frames of the relata. Donnelly's relative positionalism is the nearest neighbor (relational properties had relative to the relata), but it relativizes positions, not frames, and has no qualifier. This is the strongest single connection I found: your proposal answers a problem the literature has named and left open, with machinery the literature doesn't have.
Peirce, and F(i) == F[(i)]. The triadic sign is the closest historical ancestor of the whole architecture: semiosis is a "cooperation of three subjects — a sign, its object, and its interpretant — this trirelative influence not being in any way resolvable into actions between pairs," and Peirce's Reduction Thesis holds that genuinely triadic relations cannot be analyzed into monadic and dyadic ones. The interpretant is your point about internalizing the interpreter: perspective begins when the third correlate is inside the relation rather than standing outside it as a model-theoretic interpretation function. And Peirce's definition is itself generative in the way F(i) == F[(i)] wants to be — the interpretant "is determined to be the First Correlate of the same triadic relation to the same Object, for some possible Interpretant" — the interpretant is itself a sign, spawning the chain. Two bounds worth naming. First, Peirce cuts his taxonomy by arity (monad/dyad/triad); your dichotomy cuts by two-things versus one-thing within a fixed ternary form — adjacent taxonomies, not the same one, and I found no Peircean enumeration of the position-identification structure that yields your ten referents. Second, the literature itself flags the gap: "despite its cult status, the Peircean sign has never revealed its true potential by being integrated into a formal system".
One more tradition for the one-thing side: type-free property theory. Bealer, Cocchiarella, Turner and others argued that linguistic and ontological data are best handled by type-free property theories in which properties are a special sort of individuals predicable of other individuals via a predication relation π(x,y) — self-application admitted, Russell dodged by restricting comprehension. SRT dodges differently: there is no comprehension schema at all; referents are posited, not comprehended from formulas. That difference in how existence enters separates SRT from the entire type-free family.
The retrieval summary, stated as bounds: the relation-in-domain move is established (HiLog, Common Logic, RDF, type-free property theory); the witness-identity, the two-things/one-thing dichotomy generating a referent vocabulary, and the frame-splitting of symmetric most-specifics did not turn up anywhere; and the nearest total ancestor is Peirce, who has the irreducible triad and the internalized interpretant but no first-order axiomatization — a gap his own commentators name. If you want, the next retrieval pass could go depth-first on Fine 2000 and Donnelly, since that's where your symmetric/frame proposal would make contact with working philosophers fastest.

Let me say the five back as I now understand them, in the context of the subject-object relationship.
The subject-object relationship is the full two-thing form: subject, object, and the relationship between them, three referents all distinct, with relationship == (subject, object) — the relationship is nothing other than the most specific relationship of that pair. This is the context because it's the maximal case: every role of the primitive occupied by something other. The other four structures are what the semantics demands once you take seriously that the relationship is itself a referent — that your ternary relation is about relationship as such.
On the relational side, the differentiation happens by the relating itself stepping into one of the two roles it mediates — while two-ness is preserved, because losing two-ness wouldn't give a more specific relationship, it would give no relationship at all. Reference is the relating in the subject role: reference =reference> referent. A reference is exhausted by its referring — there is nothing to a reference besides its directedness at the referent — so the reference is the subject of its own relating, and reference == (reference, referent) says its relating to its referent is itself, not some further relating. The referent stays irreducibly other; that otherness is constitutive. Representation is the relating in the object role: representative =representation> representation. What a representative presents is its representation — the content is what's given, and the referent is reached through it. And since representations exist to refer, the inheritance chain representative -> representation -> reference -> relationship reads as the unfolding of one type of relationship into the machinery by which meaning becomes expressible: to represent is to refer by means of a content. Reference internalizes the relating on the from-side; representation on the to-side; together they expand the bare subject-object relationship into semantics.
On the identificational side: identification is one thing standing in a relating that is still other than it — identity =identification> identity, the act of recognizing a thing as itself, where the act remains distinct from the thing. Individuality is where that last distinction goes: identification and identity merge, individual =individual> individual with individual == (individual, individual) — the individual's self-identification is the individual, all three positions one referent, the terminus of the one-thing branch. And individual -> identity because every individual is an identity, though not every identity has achieved individuality.
That's ten referents, and the count is forced: three from the full form, then each subsequent structure introduces only what its position-occupation requires — two for reference, two for representation, two for identification, one for individuality.
On your metalogical observation — the retrieval sharpened it for me. Everyone who has formalized relations-as-referents treats relationship as the unanalyzed medium. Tarski-Givant algebraize operations on arbitrary relations; Peirce classifies by arity; Fine asks how an arbitrary relation applies to its relata; HiLog and Common Logic quote relations into the domain and stop there. In every case, that a relating stands between a subject and an object is the primitive fact nobody opens up. Your five structures open exactly that: they are the factorization of relationality itself, by the ways the relating can stand to what it relates. That is why nobody has done it — you can only factorize the subject-object relationship if the relationship is a referent of the same theory, and the traditions that achieved the second never asked the first question.

Working through it analytically, in chunks. I'll mark what I believe is a theorem in the current axioms versus what is my candidate construction.
Chunk 1 — The two directions are not symmetric
The relation position already has a polymorphism theorem: if x =t> y and t -> t', then x =t'> y, directly from the base reading of ->. Generalizing the relation position is always free. So the entire problem lives in the other direction: substituting more specific referents into the subject and object positions. That's never free — it's the assertion of a new relating, and the question is when the theory licenses it.
Chunk 2 — Reduction Theorem: substitution is pair-inheritance
Given x =(x,y)> y, ask when x' =(x,y)> y'.
(⇐) Suppose x' and y' stand in some relationship, so (x',y') exists with x' =(x',y')> y' by Specification, and suppose (x',y') -> (x,y). Then by the definition of ->, x' =(x,y)> y'.
(⇒) Suppose x' =(x,y)> y'. Then x' and y' stand in relationship (x,y), so by Specification (x',y') exists and inherits into every relationship the pair stands in — in particular (x',y') -> (x,y).
So: ␀0␀ ⟺ ␀1␀. Relational polymorphism is the question of when most-specificity inherits between pairs. Note what the derivation did not use: x' -> x and y' -> y appear nowhere. The componentwise arrows are neither necessary nor sufficient. They're the typing discipline that makes a substitution a candidate; the license is the pair arrow.
Chunk 3 — Your pointed arrow is the exact unit
For the theorem above, only one instance of (x',y') -> (x,y) was consumed: the instance at the pair itself. So the pointed form — reading s -(x,y)> t as x =s> y =|> x =t> y, inheritance tested at a specific pair — is precisely the minimal license: (x',y') -(x',y')> (x,y) if and only if the substitution goes through. Global -> is the universal closure of pointed arrows over all pairs. This is the "bubbling upward": a relationship type is subject-polymorphic as a global fact exactly when the pointed license holds at every pair where it's tested. The pointed arrow is where polymorphism is decided; global -> is where it accumulates.
Chunk 4 — The naive axiom is the inconsistency you warned about
The tempting axiom — x' -> x && y' -> y =|> (x',y') -> (x,y) — is exactly the incorrect specification. Grandfather kills it: Abe -> person, Ned -> person, and the naive axiom would force (Abe, Ned) -> (grandfather, grandson), making arbitrary men grandfather-related. So componentwise inheritance must never entail pair inheritance by logic alone. The license has to be carried by structure — which is Chunk 6.
Chunk 5 — Variance signatures of the five
Each pattern behaves differently under substitution, and the difference falls out of which positions are identified. A rule first, forced by the patterns themselves: identified positions substitute simultaneously. You cannot specialize one occurrence of a merged referent and leave the other.
Relationship (all distinct): the generic case. Both positions specialize covariantly, gated pair-by-pair by the Reduction Theorem. employer =(employer, employee)> manager iff (employer, manager) -> (employer, employee).
Reference (reference =reference> referent): subject and relation are identified, so specializing the subject rides the free relation-position theorem — if reference' -> reference then reference' =reference'> referent gives reference' =reference> referent immediately. Subject-covariance is a theorem, cost-free. The object is rigid: a reference to animal is not a reference to dog, because the reference is exhausted by its directedness at its referent — substitute the referent and you have destroyed the reference rather than specialized it. Signature: subject free, object invariant.
Representation (x =r> r): object and relation are identified, so they substitute together — and set theory shows this is exactly right. Let r' be the set of dogs, r the set of animals, r' -> r (membership inclusion is the inheritance). From x =r'> r', relation-generalization gives x =r> r' — member of the subset, related by superset-membership to the subset — and the simultaneous lift of the identified object position gives x =r> r: member of the subset is member of the superset. The representative position, by contrast, is rigid: poodle -> dog does not put poodle in a set that contains dog. Signature: object covariant (simultaneously with relation), subject invariant. Reference and representation are exact mirrors, which is what your conundrum about their frame-dependence would predict.
Identification (identity =identification> identity): subject and object identified, so they substitute together, and here the license is transitivity of ␀1␀ itself. If x -> y (minimally x =y> x) and x' -> x, then x' -> y, so x' =y> x'. Identification is fully polymorphic downward, and the proof is the transitivity of inheritance. This is why your minimal form works: identification is the fixed point where polymorphism and inheritance are the same operation. The asymmetric unfolding into property semantics behaves accordingly: man =(man, hair)> hair, and specializing to a particular man requires specializing exactly the identifying properties — (man', hair') -> (man, hair) demands the hair-color-level correspondences and nothing else. Gene-level: each property its own interface, and only the identifying genes get subclassed.
Individuality (all identified): total simultaneous substitution. x' -> x gives x' its own individuality — nothing carries over from x; individuality is polymorphically nuclear. But generalize just the relation position of x' =x'> x' along x' -> x and you get x' =x> x' — which is the minimal form of identification. Freeing one identified position of individuality yields identification; freeing one identified position of reference or representation yields the general relationship. The five patterns form a lattice under position-freeing, individuality at the bottom, relationship at the top, and polymorphic substitution at a specific referent bubbles up that lattice by exactly the positions it frees.
Chunk 6 — What part of the graph must be subclassed: the ancestor cone, gene by gene
Now the static analysis. Suppose x' =(x,y)> y' is asserted. For every ancestor c with (x,y) -> c, relation-generalization yields x' =c> y' as a consequence. So the substitution silently asserts the primed pair into the entire ancestor cone of (x,y). That gives the admissibility condition:
Candidate law. The substitution x' =(x,y)> y' is admissible iff every ancestor c of (x,y) admits x' =c> y' — including every referent whose existence the ancestors' axioms demand. The part of the graph that must be subclassed is exactly the ancestor cone of (x,y), restricted to those ancestors whose axioms mention the substituted positions; ancestors not mentioning them are shared unchanged.
Grandfather, worked. The canonical structure: grandparent =grandparenthood> grandchild, with the two-generation axiom as demanded existence — E[m]: grandparent =parenthood> m && m =parenthood> grandchild — and grandfatherhood -> grandparenthood with grandfather -> male. To assert Abe =(grandfather, grandson)> Bart, the cone forces: Abe -> male, Bart -> male, and — the crucial part — the existential axiom re-demands its referent at the specific level: some Homer with Abe =parenthood> Homer =parenthood> Bart, which in turn requires (Abe, Homer) -> (parent, child) and (Homer, Bart) -> (parent, child). The substitution at one relationship forces the minting of a new referent and two further pair-inheritances. That's your prediction confirmed in miniature: fully characterizing the new referents needed is the transitive closure of demanded-existence through the cone, and it can cascade — the complexity is real and structural, not an artifact.
Chunk 7 — Where contravariance actually lives
Specification-guided check. Take vet =treats> animal and dogVet =treats> dog. The relatings include upward fine: every treating of a dog by a dog-vet is a treating of an animal by a vet — relationships are covariant in both positions under ->. But dogVet -> vet as role inheritance fails: the vet role promises vet =treats> cat, and dogVet cannot carry it. So the contravariance you flagged does not attach to the relationship arrow at all — it attaches to the role arrows. A role is usable in place of a more general role only if it accepts everything the general role accepts: the accepted side of a role contravaries, while the relationship's own positions covary. The variance annotations other type systems stipulate per-parameter are, here, derived: a position's variance is determined by which of the five patterns it participates in — identification-positions free by transitivity, reference-subjects free by identification with the relation, reference-objects and representation-subjects invariant, everything else covariant gated by pointed pair-inheritance, with role-acceptance carrying the contravariant burden.

The next chunk I'd propose: run the cone law against representation specifically — subset chains are the cleanest closed graphs of most-specific relationships we have, and if the law is right, it should reproduce exactly the subset/member/superset entailments and nothing more.

Substitutions to try for `x =(x,y)> y`: S1 swap subject only: x' =(x,y)> y (x' -> x) S2 swap object only: x =(x,y)> y' (y' -> y) S3 swap both, unrelated: x' =(x,y)> y' S4 swap both, corresponding: x' =(x',y')> y' with (x',y') -> (x,y) S6 relationship specialized: x =(x,y)'> y Legend: ✓ guaranteed (polymorphic) · holds only by luck ✗ fails (asserts false) =============================================================================== ## ROLE SEMANTICS FIRST (use the semantics of the role) =============================================================================== A role like `lock` is DEFINED by: the thing whose most specific relationship INCLUDES being-opened-by-its-key. `lock` is the object-role of `opens`. Every actual lock inherits into it. The role is `(key, lock)` seen from the object side. If a role is defined THROUGH the relationship, the two roles of a coupled relationship are defined TOGETHER — you can't specify one without the other. Naive test: CAN THE ROLE BE DEFINED WITHOUT THE OTHER ROLE? eats: eater alone? yes. eaten alone? yes. → looks UNCOUPLED opens: key-of-a-lock, lock-openable-by-key. → COUPLED owns: owner needs an owned; owned needs an owner. → looks COUPLED (We will see this NAMING test is the wrong test.) =============================================================================== ## RELATIONSHIP 1: eats (candidate UNCOUPLED) =============================================================================== Roles: eater, eaten. Base: eater =(eater,eaten)> eaten. Fat: cat->eater, cow->eater, mouse->eaten, grass->eaten. S1 subject only: cat =(eater,eaten)> eaten "a cat eats edible things" ✓ S2 object only: eater =(eater,eaten)> mouse "eaters eat mice" ✓ S3 both free: cat =(eater,eaten)> grass "cat eats grass" ✓ cow =(eater,eaten)> mouse "cow eats mouse" · FALSE in world >>> S3 does NOT hold in general. A COMPATIBILITY constraint hides here: eaten must be edible-BY-this-eater. Roles separately nameable, NOT independently substitutable. cat+grass ok, cow+mouse not. S4 corresponding: herbivore =(herbivore,plant)> plant ✓ S6 relation spec: cat =(grazes)> grass (grazing ⊂ eating) ✓ grazing FORCES object=plant — specializing the RELATIONSHIP constrained the OBJECT. The axes are not independent. LESSON 1: "uncoupled" was wrong. eater/eaten carry a compatibility relation. Separable-to-name ≠ independent-to-substitute. =============================================================================== ## RELATIONSHIP 2: opens (COUPLED) =============================================================================== Roles: key-of, lock-of, co-defined. Base: key =(key,lock)> lock. S1 subject only: car-key =(key,lock)> lock "car-key opens locks" ✗ false S2 object only: key =(key,lock)> padlock "keys open padlocks" ✗ false S3 both free: car-key =(key,lock)> padlock ✗ false S4 corresponding: car-key =(car-key,car-lock)> car-lock ✓ ONLY this S6 relation spec: key =(unlocks-deadbolt)> deadbolt — drags BOTH roles ✓ LESSON 2: coupled ⇒ only S4. The correspondence is forced by the roles being mutually most-specific. =============================================================================== ## RELATIONSHIP 3: owns (the instructive surprise) =============================================================================== Roles: owner, owned. Base: owner =(owner,owned)> owned. S1 subject only: landlord =(owner,owned)> owned "landlord owns things" ✓ S2 object only: owner =(owner,owned)> building "owners own buildings" ✓ S3 both free: landlord =(owner,owned)> building ✓ >>> owns behaves UNCOUPLED even though naming `owner` needs `owns`. Co-NAMING did NOT create co-SUBSTITUTION. LESSON 3: coupling-for-SUBSTITUTION ≠ co-definition-for-NAMING. owner/owned are co-named but substitute independently; key/lock are co-named AND co-substitute. So the §-earlier role-definition test is NOT the coupling test. =============================================================================== ## WHAT ACTUALLY SEPARATES owns FROM opens? =============================================================================== opens: a specific key fits a specific lock — a FURTHER most-specific relationship between the two instances (cuts match pins). Object instance determined by subject instance. owns: a specific owner and owned thing need NO further relationship. Free. >>> COUPLING CRITERION: Coupled ⟺ the two roles stand in a FURTHER most-specific relationship c that every valid (x,y) must instance. In SRT: exists `(x,y) -> c` BEYOND the relationship itself, jointly constraining x and y. If yes → narrowing x must preserve c, forcing corresponding y. If no → positions covary independently. The "part of the graph to subclass" = the ancestors c that jointly constrain both positions. =============================================================================== ## RELATIONSHIP 4: north-of (converse / perspective) =============================================================================== Roles: norther, souther. a =(a,b)> b = "a north of b". Converse: b =(b,a)> a = "b south of a" — SAME fact, other frame. Coupling is TOTAL but is PURE DIRECTION, no further constraint c. This is the symmetric/perspective case: north-of and south-of are the two most-specifics, equal modulo perspective — one in F[a], one in F[b] (Doug's conjecture). >>> TWO SOURCES OF COUPLING: (i) constraint-coupling: shared further ancestor c (key/lock, grandfather). (ii) converse-coupling: relationship is its own converse up to perspective (north/south, spouse, twin). Positions co-vary as the same pair reversed. =============================================================================== ## RELATIONSHIP 5: grandfather-of (constraint + DEMANDED middle) =============================================================================== Roles: grandfather, grandson. Base carries E[m]: gf =parent> m =parent> gs. Only S4, and specializing an endpoint re-demands m (m'->m). Constraint-coupling where c is EXISTENTIAL — the strongest form. Subclass cost = the demanded chain. =============================================================================== ## ENUMERATED PATTERN TABLE =============================================================================== | relationship | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | coupling type | |--------------|-----|-----|---------|-------------|---------------------| | owns | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | none (free) | | eats | ✓ | ✓ | · compat| ✓ | compatibility | | opens | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | constraint | | grandfather | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ + demand | constraint + exist. | | north-of | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ converse | converse/perspective| =============================================================================== ## LAW (candidate — enumerated, not asserted) =============================================================================== For `x =(x,y)> y`, a position substitution is polymorphically GUARANTEED iff it preserves every ancestor `(x,y) -> c`. - No ancestor c binds x,y jointly (owns): independent covariance; S1,S2,S3,S4 ✓. - c is a COMPATIBILITY predicate (eats): free within c's satisfiers; S3 only for compatible pairs. - c BINDS the two instances (opens): only S4 (joint corresponding, preserving c). - c is EXISTENTIAL/demanded (grandfather): S4 plus re-supply of demanded referent. - coupling is CONVERSE (north-of): S4 as same pair reversed; the two most-specifics split across F[x], F[y]. Variance is DERIVED per relationship from its ancestor cone: positions covary jointly exactly along shared ancestors, independently exactly where there are none. =============================================================================== ## OPEN / TO CHECK WITH DOUG =============================================================================== 1. Is compatibility-coupling (eats) distinct from constraint-coupling, or the SAME mechanism at lower strength? I suspect one law, a spectrum in how much c constrains — owns(none) → eats(compat) → opens(binding) → grandfather(exist.). 2. Confirm the correction: coupling is shared ANCESTORS, not shared NAMING. 3. Does perspective enter EXACTLY when c is the converse? That would tie the symmetric-most-specific conjecture directly to this enumeration. ENDOFDOC echo "written"; wc -l relational_polymorphism.md

I ran it like code — every substitution on every relationship, marked hold or fail with the sentence as the test. Three things fell out that I couldn't see from the armchair.
"Uncoupled" doesn't exist the way I claimed. I set up eats as the clean independent case, and S3 immediately failed: "cow eats mouse" is false. eater and eaten are separately nameable but not independently substitutable — there's a compatibility constraint (the eaten must be edible by the eater) hiding in the pair. Separable-to-name is not independent-to-substitute. That killed my earlier framing on contact with one bad sentence.
Co-naming is not co-substitution — this is the real correction. I had proposed (your §5 role-definition point, which I'd taken as a coupling test) that being defined through the relationship makes roles coupled. owns refutes it cleanly: owner needs "owns" to be named, owned needs it too — fully co-named — yet S1, S2, S3 all hold. A landlord owns things, owners own buildings, a landlord owns a building, all guaranteed. So coupling for substitution is not about shared naming. When I asked what actually separates owns from opens, the answer was concrete: a specific key fits a specific lock — there's a further most-specific relationship between the two instances (cuts match pins) — whereas a specific owner and owned thing require no further relationship at all. Anyone can own anything; not any key opens any lock.
That gives the coupling criterion in SRT's own terms. Coupled iff the two roles stand in a further most-specific relationship c that every valid pair must instance — iff there's (x,y) -> c beyond the relationship itself that constrains x and y jointly. Then the whole variance table is derived, not annotated: no such c → independent covariance (owns); c a compatibility predicate → free within its satisfiers (eats); c binding the instances → only the joint corresponding narrowing holds (opens); c existential → that plus re-supplying the demanded referent (grandfather). And the static-analysis payoff you wanted: the part of the graph you must subclass is exactly the ancestors c that jointly constrain both positions — follow those, leave the rest shared.
The north-of row is the one I want to flag toward your perspective work. Its coupling is total but carries no constraint c — it's pure direction, the relationship as its own converse. So there look to be two kinds of coupling: constraint-coupling (a shared ancestor) and converse-coupling (the same pair reversed), and the second is exactly where north-of/south-of become the two most-specifics equal modulo perspective, one landing in F[a], one in F[b].
So the sharp question, which is open item 1: is compatibility-coupling really its own kind, or is it constraint-coupling turned down low — one law with a spectrum in how much c constrains, running owns (none) → eats (compatibility) → opens (binding) → grandfather (existential)? If that's one mechanism, the law is a single statement about the ancestor cone. And item 3, the one I find most promising: does perspective enter exactly when c is the converse — which would tie your symmetric-most-specific conjecture directly to this enumeration rather than leaving it a separate posit?

Yes — I see it, and I see exactly where my S6 row was incoherent. Let me state it back plainly, because this is the thing to verify before any plan.
(x,y) is the most specific relationship of x and y. Therefore nothing more specific can ever hold between x and y themselves — x =(x',y')> y is forbidden by definition, and my S6 ("specialize the relationship, hold the pair fixed") asked for precisely that impossibility. Mother and daughter: mother =mother-of> daughter, and no specialization of mother-of will ever apply to those two — they already have their most specific. Specialization only ever lives at a new pair.
So the direction runs the opposite way. x' =(x,y)> y' is literally r(x',y') — passing specialized arguments into the relationship. But r can't be their most specific, since they're specialized — they need their own (x',y') -> (x,y). Which gives the whole content in one implication:
x' =(x',y')> y' =|> x' =(x,y)> y'
And yes, that is equivalent to polymorphism — it's subsumption exactly: an instance of the specialized relationship is an instance of the general one, arguments of subtypes passed where the supertype relationship is expected, truth flowing upward from the specific pair through every ancestor. "Specialized correctly" means(x',y') -> (x,y) holds — that inheritance is the Liskov condition in SRT's terms. And the equality corollary closes it: x' =(x,y)> y' being most specific forces x' == x, y' == y, where the implication holds trivially.

Specializing the relationship and specializing the pair are the same act, because the relationship is (x,y). Given x =t> y for some t != eq, there exists spec such that:
x =spec> y — spec actually relates x and y (spec is a real relating of them)
A[gen: x =gen> y]: spec --> gen — spec carries every relating of x and y as a constituent (it's the richest)
gen !--> spec — and no such gen carries spec back (nothing else is as rich; this is the strictness that, with 2, does the work I was wrongly calling "antisymmetry")
!E[x',y']: (x' != x | y' != y) & x' =spec> y' — spec relates nothing but x and y; it's theirs alone

Now the real problem, and you're right that it's a genuine contradiction as I set it up. Let me not wriggle — let me find where the reasoning breaks.
I claimed: r is relational (distinct pairs), i is individual (self), and a mixed thing can inherit from neither. But you've just pointed out that every referent in the global frame carries minimal individuality — x =x> x, the bare "I can be identified at all." So every referent inherits from i. And every referent that relates to anything else inherits from r. So the generic case is inheriting from both — which my T9 declared impossible. The contradiction is real and it's mine.
Here's where I think the error is. I treated r and i as partitioning by pairs — as if a relationship inherits from r only if all its pairs are distinct, from i only if all are self. That "all its pairs" test is the smuggled set-theoretic move again: I was quantifying over the extension of a relationship as if inheritance were about the whole tuple-set matching. But inheritance is genetic — per gene, per site, exactly the thing you've been correcting. x =x> x is not "the relationship t has an all-self extension." It's: at this referent, the individuality gene is expressed. And x =r> y at a distinct relating is the relationship gene expressed there.
So the resolution: i and r are not competing classes that a relationship must fall into wholesale. They are two genes, and a referent can express both — individuality minimally (it can be identified at all) and relationship (it stands in relatings to others). There is no dichotomy at the level of "which one do you inherit from." The dichotomy is between two forms of expression at a site: a relating with x = y expresses the i-gene there; a relating with x ≠ y expresses the r-gene there. Same referent, both genes, different sites. My T9 mistook "the top splits into two genes" for "each referent picks one top," and those are completely different claims.
Which means the thing I proved isn't false, it was mis-stated. What's true: no single relating site is both a self-relating and a distinct-relating (x=y and x≠y can't both hold at one site — that much is real, it's just !=). What's false: that this forces a referent to inherit from only one top. The site-level exclusivity is real; the referent-level exclusivity I derived from it was the error, produced by quantifying over extensions.
So the dichotomy is genuinely a dichotomy of relatings (a given relating is either self or distinct, never both), and emphatically not a dichotomy of referents or of inheritance. Every referent in the global frame expresses i (minimal individuality, x =x> x) and typically also r (it relates to others). The bear's minimal x =x> x is the i-gene; the bear eating a fish is the r-gene; nothing stops one bear from carrying both.

Let me hold the four-part axiom and work through what you've actually handed me, because there are several distinct things here and I don't want to blur them.
First, the graph picture, because it reorganizes everything. SRT is a graph where the edge is also a node — the relating is a referent, so it sits in the graph as a thing that other relatings can point at. Individuality is what earns a referent a circle on the graph at all: x =x> x is the loop that says "there is a node here, capable of being identified." And the full expression of all three — leaving from a node, passing through, arriving back — is the infinity figure through a single node. That's the picture I should be reasoning from, not "genes." Genetics was only ever a metaphor forper-site expression, and the real thing it was pointing at is: the graph has local structure at each relating, and inheritance is a statement about that structure.
And here's what I think you're telling me inheritance actually is, structurally: it says there's one spot where the graph mirrors itself — where x =s> y forces x =t> y, the s-structure is echoed in the t-structure at that site. What it does not tell you is what the rest of the graph must look like for that mirroring to be possible. That's the deep open thing: the most specific relationship gives you the skeleton, and inheritance says "there's a mirror here," but what symmetry the mirror forces on the rest of the graph is unknown and probably profound — quite possibly a lens through which most SRT theorems are secretly about forced graph structure. Which is exactly why getting -> right matters: it's not bookkeeping, it's the thing that determines what structure is forced.
Now the not-relationship, which is where I think the real result is, and let me state it carefully because you gave me the proof.
In ordinary logic you can write x ⇒ y ⇒ z and, if you can assert the existence of such a mediating y, relate x and z directly — transitivity closes the gap. SRT does not do this, and shouldn't. "word" refers to any word; "salmon" refers to an actual salmon; the salmon-word refers to the fish you caught in Wyoming. Should the graph therefore relate "word" to that fish? No. They are related only through the mediating referents, and SRT does not force the graph to be closed under that composition. The relating is real at each step; the composite is not automatically a relating.
That's the essential not-a-relationship: composition-in-general is not itself a relationship in SRT. And you can prove it can't be, which is the theorem you pointed at. Suppose "not-a-relationship" — or the general composite — were a relationship. If it relates two distinct referents, then by D1 it must inherit from relationship (r). But its whole content is that it is not one — it fails to be the kind of thing that inherits from r. Contradiction. So SRT does not admit every logical permutation as a relationship: the things that would have to inherit from r while denying they're relational simply don't exist in the graph. Non-closure isn't a limitation; it's forced by the theory's own account of what a relationship is.
This is why the four-part axiom is precious to you, and I now see the shape of why. If the most specific relationship exists if and only if x and y genuinely relate — not through a mediator, not by logical permutation, but actually — then the axiom is holding the line between identification and logic itself. It says: the graph only has the node-for-the-edge where there is a real relating, and logic's free composition does not get to manufacture edges. That's the essential thing about the relationship between identification and logic that you don't want to lose by collapsing the axiom into something weaker. So I'll hold it — an F that exists if and only if x and y relate — as a candidate we protect, precisely because the biconditional is where the elegance lives.

Let me lay out exactly where -> stands, formally, and then give you the decision that has to be made — because I don't think I can make it for you, but I can make it precise.
The problem with forward-only. Define s -> t :: A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y. This is materially too weak, and here is the exact failure. Take any s that refers nothing — no x,y with x =s> y. Then the antecedent is always false, the implication always vacuously true, and s -> t for every t. An empty relating inherits everything. More generally, wherever s and t are jointly silent on a pair, that pair contributes a vacuous truth, so the sparser s is, the more it vacuously inherits. That's the vacuity you flagged.
What your antisymmetry proposal was reaching for. You proposed (s -> t ∧ t -> s) =|> s == t. We then found — the grandfather case — that this cannot be a universal law, because combined with a universal r it forces subject and object to share inheritance and collapses (x,y) onto the diagonal. So the reverse-collapse is dead as stated. But notice: killing reverse-collapse does nothing about the vacuity problem. Vacuity is a defect in the forward half. Antisymmetry was addressing a different worry (too many identities), not the vacuity (too many inheritances). So we have two separate issues and the antisymmetry patch never touched the first one.
The formal diagnosis. Vacuity comes from letting the forward implication be satisfied by absence. The fix must require that inheritance is witnessed by presence — t inherits from s only if s actually does referring for t to be present in. In SRT terms: s -> t should mean not merely "no s-referring lacks t" but "t is genuinely part of what s does." That points at a grounding clause: -> must be anchored by at least one actual relating.
Here are the three formally distinct repairs, and I'll be honest that choosing among them is a semantic decision about SRT that is yours:
Option A — grounded forward. s -> t :: (E[x,y]: x =s> y) ∧ (A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y) Read: s actually refers something, and everywhere s refers, t refers. This kills vacuity from empty s. Reflexivity holds for any non-silent s. But it has a cost: a relating that refers nothing inherits nothing, not even itself — x =x> x would need x to actually self-refer for x -> x. Given individuality earns the node, that may be exactly right.
Option B — per-site grounding (the pointed arrow as primitive). s -(x,y)> t :: x =s> y ∧ x =t> y — inheritance at a named relating, presence on both sides, no implication at all, so no vacuity possible. Then global s -> t is not the universal closure (you said non-transitive-closure; universal closure over sites reintroduces vacuous sites). Instead global -> would be defined only where you want it, built up from pointed facts. This matches your "genetic/per-site" intuition most closely and structurally cannot go vacuous, because it never uses an implication.
Option C — forward + witnessed-overlap. s -> t :: (A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y) ∧ (E[x,y]: x =s> y ∧ x =t> y) Read: everywhere s refers t refers, and there's at least one relating where both actually fire. The second conjunct is the presence-witness that blocks vacuity while keeping the universal forward clause.
My formal recommendation, for you to accept or reject. Options A and C both cure vacuity; they differ only in whether the witness must cover all of s (A) or merely exist (C). Since your (x,y) machinery (A3 clause ii) already quantifies "inherits every relating of x,y," the universal forward clause is load-bearing there — so C preserves A3 unchanged while curing vacuity, whereas A weakens the universal reading. B is the deepest and most SRT-native, but it changes what -> fundamentally is (a per-site fact, not a global claim), and that reshapes A3 and everything downstream.

And it's far too weak: "cat eats mouse" and "cat chases mouse" share the relating-site cat-to-mouse, so eats -> chases and chases -> eats both hold. Overlap is not inheritance. Inheritance was supposed to say everywhere s fires, t fires — the universal forward clause carried the whole directional, containment content. What this tells us about the most foundational form. The two requirements are now sharp and they pull in opposite directions:
Directionality/containment needs the universal: A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y.
Non-vacuity needs a presence-witness: E[x,y]: x =s> y ∧ x =t> y.
Neither alone suffices — A alone goes vacuous, E alone goes symmetric. The foundational expression is theirconjunction, which is exactly Option C from before, now derived rather than proposed:
srt
s -> t  ::  (A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y)  ∧  (E[x,y]: x =s> y ∧ x =t> y)

s -> t  ::  (E[x,y]: x =s> y)  ∧  (A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y)
That is Option A — grounded forward — and we've now shown A and C are the same definition, because the universal clause makes the two witness-forms equivalent. That convergence is the sign we've hit something foundational: two different-looking repairs turn out identical once you use the forward clause. The single most foundational reading:
␀0␀ holds when s actually refers something, and everywhere s refers, t refers there too.
Non-vacuous (s must fire at least once), directional (the A is not symmetric), and it makes s -> s hold exactly for the relatings that are not empty — which ties directly to individuality: a relating earns its self-inheritance by actually referring, the same way individuality x =x> x earns the node. Silence inherits nothing, not even itself.

Whether every referent in the global frame refers at least itself (x =x> x always present) then becomes the question of whether -> is totally reflexive — and that's precisely the individuality/i question from §6, now sharpened: total reflexivity of -> ⟺ every referent self-refers. So this definition doesn't decide the individuality question, itreduces to it, which is where it should bottom out.

The web search confirms the logical structure I derived is standard, and one result is directly on point. The vacuous-truth mechanism is exactly as I used it: a universal statement that can be converted to a conditional statement is true because the antecedent cannot be satisfied, and if there are no Ps, we consider P ⇒ Q to be true, regardless of whether there are any Qs. So s -> t going vacuously true when s has no subject-relatings is the textbook vacuity, and individuality is precisely the fact that removes the empty-antecedent case. The Horn-formula result (index 7) confirms the shape: an atomic proposition is of the form (xRy), and a Horn clause x₁ ∧ ... ∧ xₙ ⟹ y is the natural frame-language form — which is exactly what x =s> y =|> x =t> y is, a Horn clause over the relation R. So -> is a universal Horn clause over R, and that's a well-understood object.
Now the results, brought back from the scratchpad — and the headline is that your intuition is right but the direction matters.
␀0␀ and ␀1␀ are not equivalent — but ␀2␀ implies ␀3␀, and that implication is a theorem. The proof is three lines: assume s -> t, which is A[x,y]: x =s> y =|> x =t> y. Individuality gives s =s> s. Instantiate the universal at x:=s, y:=s: s =s> s =|> s =t> s. Modus ponens delivers s =t> s. So (s -> t) & individuality ⟹ s =t> s. That is the theorem you wanted — the identification form falls out of the inheritance form, because a thing identifies itself. Individuality is the bridge that turns "t holds everywhere s does" into "t holds at s's own identification."
The reverse fails, and I have a counter-model (M2): four referents, with s =t> s holding but a =s> b true while a =t> b false. There s =t> s holds and s -> t fails at (a,b). So s =t> s does not give you s -> t — knowing t holds at the diagonal point tells you nothing about the off-diagonal relatings. This means s -> t is strictly stronger: it's "t everywhere s relates," and s =t> s is just its restriction to the single self-relating point.
On your two direct questions. Is it a theorem or the definition? The clean logical picture is: the universal Horn form is thedefinition, and s =t> s is the theorem it yields (given individuality). It "sort of implies it" exactly — not equivalence, implication, one-directional, provable. And does individuality rescue vacuity? Precisely and only. Material implication alone is not enough — it goes vacuous. But individuality guarantees every referent has at least the subject-relating s =s> s, so the antecedent is never empty, so s -> t always carries real content: at minimum s =t> s. So "implication is minimally enough" is equivalent to "individuality holds." The adequacy of the definition rides entirely on D2/individuality.
One caveat I have to flag rather than bury: all of this is the global frame, where individuality is guaranteed. Your notebooks have self-relation withdrawn in specific frames — and there the antecedent at (s,s) is gone, s -> t no longer forces s =t> s, and vacuity can return frame-locally. So the equivalence-as-theorem is frame-relative.
The open question for you, which the logic can't decide on its own: the clean finding makes the universal form definitional and s =t> s the theorem. Do you want it that way, or do you want s =t> s closer to definitional with the universal "everywhere s relates" form derived? The former is what the logic supports directly; the latter would need extra structure to recover the "everywhere" from the single diagonal point.

Worked it on the scratchpad. The answer to "what's missing" turned out to have two layers, and the first one killed my easy guesses before the real thing showed up.
First, what doesn't close the gap. I tried the obvious move — maybe identification-inheritance was never supposed to range over all x,y, only the diagonal, so define s ->_id t :: x =s> x =|> x =t> x. But counter-model M3 breaks even that: two self-relatings s =t> s and c =s> c with c =t> c absent, and s =t> s still doesn't give the diagonal-only arrow. So the gap is not diagonal-versus-all. It's one point versus all points — s =t> s is a single relating, and any -> is a universal, and one instance never yields a universal without a principle carrying it across referents. That's the honest core of why it fails, and it's why no amount of restricting the quantifier fixes it.
Then the thing that does close it, and it comes straight from the graph picture you've been insisting on — the edge is a node. The missing ingredient is that s has to be read as the relating itself — the node that is an edge — not as a bare referent. M2 broke the equivalence precisely by usings as a bare referent with an unrelated a =s> b hanging off it. But if s is a relating, then a =s> b means (a,b) = s, and a and b live under s. The bridge that then ties it together:
␀0␀ — a relationship inherits t exactly when the underlying relating holds.
The ⟸ direction is already A3's immediate theorem in the kit. The ⟹ direction is the one I want you to check, because it's blocked from failing only by the §3 biconditional: a relationship (a,b) inheriting t without a =t> b would be an edge-node carrying a relating that doesn't hold — which the biconditional ("the graph gets the edge-node exactly where there is genuine relating") forbids. So M4, the counter-model I tried to build against the bridge, is blocked.
So the answer to your question: what ␀0␀ is missing is the §3 biconditional. s =t> s alone is one relating and can't reach the universal. It becomes identification-complete only whens is the relating-as-node and you use the bridge (x,y) -> t ⟺ x =t> y — and that bridge is licensed by nothing other than the biconditional you've been holding onto in §3. The diagonal of the node (m =t> m) connects to the underlying relating (x =t> y) through the biconditional, and that's what defeats M2. Identification turns out to be a fact about relatings, not bare referents — which is exactly "the edge is a node" doing real work rather than being a slogan.
The one thing I need from you before I write any of this into the kit: does the §3 biconditional license the⟹ direction of the bridge — (x,y) -> t ⟹ x =t> y? I derived that it's blocked from failing by the biconditional, but "blocked from failing" becoming "provable" is exactly the kind of step I've been wrong about, so I'm holding it as a candidate until you confirm the biconditional is meant to carry that weight.

Your worry was correct, and tracking it down was the whole payoff. Here's what the scratchpad found.
Where the universal-on-existential actually was. T-selfref itself is clean — it goes from the universal s -> t to the instance s =t> s, which is just instantiation, sound. And the kit never claims the reverse. But the bridge I proposed last turn — x =t> y ⟹ (x,y) -> t — is a universal-on-existential, exactly as you feared. (x,y) -> t unfolds to A[u,v]: u =(x,y)> v =|> u =t> v, a universal, and x =t> y is a single relating. Counter-model M5 breaks it: let (x,y) relate a second pair p,q with t absent there, and the universal fails while x =t> y holds. So I did inflate an existential into a universal. Caught.
What rescues it — and only just. M5 requires (x,y) to relate a second pair. But A3 clause (iv), exclusivity, forbids exactly that: the most-specific relating m = (x,y) relates nothing but x to y. So the universal (x,y) -> t has exactly one live instance, and it collapses to x =t> y. The bridge is sound — but only because of exclusivity, and only for most-specific relatings. Without exclusivity it's the illegitimate inflation you flagged. So the honest statement is: s =t> s gives s -> t exactly for exclusive relatings, and is false for bare referents (M2). Exclusivity is the dividing line, and that's why this is identification-specific — identification is about the relating-as-node, which is exclusive.
Your axiom question, answered. The property you described — a referent inheriting an identity inherits the ways it can be identified — I wrote as IDENT-INHERIT: (x -> s) & (s =t> s) ⟹ x =t> x. I tried to derive it and could not: from x =s> x and s =t> s there's no rule transferring t across the s-to-x identification. So your instinct is right — as written, it is not derivable and would have to be a raw axiom.
But here's the thing worth your attention, and it's the same instance-versus-universal gap you named. The only reason it needs an axiom is that you wrote identifiability as s =t> s (an instance). If identifiability is expressed instead as s -> t (the universal — "t is among what identifies s"), then downward transfer is just (x -> s) & (s -> t) ⟹ x -> t, which is T-trans — already a theorem. No new axiom at all. The entire difficulty collapses onto the choice you flagged: s =t> s versus s -> t. Transitivity already is the semantics of identification-inheritance you're worried about losing — but only if identifiability lives at the universal s -> t, not the instance s =t> s.
So the three options, cleanest first: express identifiability as s -> t and get the downward-transfer property free from transitivity, no axiom; or keep s =t> s and route through exclusivity, which only works for most-specific relatings; or add IDENT-INHERIT as an explicit axiom, which you said you're reluctant to do. The first makes your reluctance unnecessary — the property you want is already a theorem, provided identification is carried by -> rather than by the single diagonal instance.
The question that decides it, and it's yours: when you say "the ways a thing can be identified," is that inherently a universal claim (all the ways — which is s -> t), or is it meant to be witnessed instance-by-instance (s =t> s for each t)? If the former, you already have what you want and I can write it into the kit as a consequence of transitivity. If the latter, we're choosing between exclusivity-routing and a new axiom.

Fixed in three places, and the diagnosis is exactly yours. Here's what happened and why it's fatal.
I called (x,y) a "canonical function," and -> is the order on referents. A function that preserves an order is, by definition, monotonic. So by naming it a function on referents whose order is ->, I let the reader — me — slide to "canonical monotonic function." Nobody wrote "monotonic," but the two words I did write entail it if you're not careful, and I wasn't.
Why that breaks inheritance everywhere, made formal on the scratchpad: monotonicity would mean x' -> x & y' -> y ⟹ (x',y') -> (x,y) — specializing both arguments automatically specializes the output. If that held, then by T-polyevery componentwise specialization would carry the relationship. Abe → person, Ned → person would force(Abe, Ned) -> (grandfather, grandson) — arbitrary people standing in any relationship their types can. You could never specify which specializations actually inherit, because they all would, automatically. Inheritance would be entailed by argument-inheritance alone, which is the same as saying it can't be specified — "broken everywhere because you can't specify it," precisely your words.
So the correction is that (x,y) is emphatically not monotonic: (x',y') -> (x,y) is always a separate fact that must be specified, never forced by x' -> x and y' -> y. And this reframes the grandfather strike from §2 — grandfather isn't a special pathology, it's just an instance of non-monotonicity. Non-monotonicity is required for inheritance to be specifiable at all. I wrote that into the canonical-function entry, into §3 next to A3, and I guarded T-poly so its hypothesis can't be misread as coming for free.
T-poly itself survives untouched, because it only ever assumed (x',y') -> (x,y) as a hypothesis and drew a consequence — it never claimed the hypothesis was automatic. The damage was purely in the framing of the function, not in the theorem.
This connects straight back to where we were before your catch: the identifiability question. If identification-inheritance rode on the canonical function being monotonic, it'd be trivial and broken. It doesn't — which is why the downward-transfer property has to come from transitivity of -> on explicitly-specified inheritances ((x -> s) & (s -> t) ⟹ x -> t), not from the canonical function preserving anything. The non-monotonicity is what leaves room for identification to be real specification rather than automatic collapse.

You're right, and the check found something serious — the kit as written is a dead theory, and it's exactly the failure you named.
Here's the contradiction, built from a model rather than asserted. Take a genuine specialization: x' -> x, y' -> y, and ask whether the specialized pair inherits the general relationship, (x',y') -> (x,y). Because (x',y') is exclusive — it relates only x' to y' — that universal collapses to a single instance: (x',y') -> (x,y) holds iff x' =(x,y)> y'. But now look at (x,y)'s own exclusivity, clause (iv): (x,y) relates nothing but x to y. So x' =(x,y)> y' with (x',y') ≠ (x,y) is forbidden by (x,y)'s own exclusivity clause. Therefore (x',y') -> (x,y) can only hold when the pairs are identical — nothing ever inherits a most-specific relationship except itself. T-poly's hypothesis is never satisfiable. The theory is consistent with "no relationship is ever inherited," which means, as you said, it isn't a theory about inheritance at all. My compaction checked for contradictions and completely missed that the axioms jointly forbid the phenomenon they're supposed to describe.
The root cause is a mis-statement of exclusivity that I introduced. I glossed A3 clause (iv) as "m relates nothing but x to y." Read flatly, that says m may never appear as a relating of any other pair — which is what kills inheritance, because inheriting m means relating under m. The intent almost certainly is weaker: m = (x,y) is the most-specific of x,y and of no other pair — it isn't anyone else's canonical/most-specific — but other pairs can relate under m without m being their most-specific. Under that reading (call it iv′), I built a live model M6: x' =m'> y' with m' -> m, so x' =m> y' follows, inheritance actually happens, and exclusivity still holds because m is most-specific only of x,y and m' only of x',y'. Live theory.
Two honest consequences I have to flag rather than smooth over. First, fixing (iv) to (iv′) reopens the bridge from two sessions ago — (x,y) -> t ⟺ x =t> y — because that bridge's soundness relied on the too-strong exclusivity collapsing a universal to one instance. Under the correct weaker exclusivity, m can relate many pairs, the universal doesn't collapse, and the bridge may again be the universal-on-existential you originally worried about. It needs re-deriving. Second, an import I should mark: "monotonic" is an order-theory analogy — the actual SRT fact is that inheritance is not carried componentwise from parts to whole. I'll reword it as an analogy where it appears.
I haven't edited the kit yet, because the fix hinges on a reading of your axiom I shouldn't choose unilaterally. Is (iv) meant as I now suspect — ␀0␀ is the most-specific of x,y and of no other pair, but other pairs may relate under it — rather than my flat "relates nothing but x to y"? If yes, I'll correct clause (iv), mark T-poly as live, add the reduction I found ((x',y') -> (x,y) is the specification that the specialized pair relates under the general relationship), and re-open the bridge as an explicit question. If the strong reading was actually intended, then inheritance needs its machinery somewhere other than relating-under-m, and I'd need you to point me at where.

First, my method checks out against your demo. Putting the subject into the relation-position — x =x> y — is the reference pattern (subject collapses into relation), and it's a fixed point because subject = relation = x. That's your "referential version is a fixed point," reproduced. Andx =x> x is the same formula wearing two readings: as representation-of-self it's the forbidden thing (a referent strictly inside its own representation), but it's also exactly the individuality axiom. So the contradiction and its rescue are the same string, and individuality wins by axiom — the diagonal that naive set theory chokes on (x ∈ x) is, in SRT, individuality by definition. That's the mechanism of your favorite part, located precisely: SRT absorbs the diagonal paradox by making the diagonal an axiom.
Now the three placements, and they have the parallel structure you were hoping for — one level up, with the relating m = (x,y) as the referent being placed:
m =m> x — reference fixed point, subject = relation = m. The reference pattern, but now it's the relationship doing the referring.
x =m> m — representation fixed point, object = relation = m. The representation pattern, the relationship as x's representation.
m =m> m — individuality of the relating, all three slots m, and this one is forced by the individuality axiom, not optional.
So "put the most-specific m into each slot" generates reference, representation, and individuality as sub-relationships — which is the five-relationship dichotomy again, but with the relating itself as the placed referent. That's what makes it a candidate for where subject and object get their semantics: x is subject-like and y is object-like precisely by how m places itself relative to them.
And here's the result I think is genuinely important. Your third case — "every expression of individuality is most specific," m =m> m being (m,m)'s most-specific — is consistent only under the corrected exclusivity (iv′) from last turn. Under the strong (iv) I wrote, m relates other pairs so it can't be (m,m)'s most-specific, and the conjecture fails. Under (iv′) — m is most-specific of no other pair but may relate other pairs — it goes through. So the dead-theory bug and your individuality conjecture demand the same fix, independently. That's the kind of convergence that suggests (iv′) isn't a patch but the truth: two unrelated roads both require it.

Your written forms put the reference sub-relationship as m =m> x — the relationship refers to the base-subject. But your prose said "the relationship refers to the object," which would be m =m> y. Those select differently, and the choice is the definition of which of x, y is subject and which is object. Which is it — does m refer to x, or to y?

First, the correction you caught: clause (ii) is not an extra obligation for (z,z)==z — it's part of what "most-specific" means. So (z,z)==z stands on the definition, not on a side-proof. Fixed, and I dropped my caveat.
Now the substitutions. Reference, representation, and individuality all behave as fixed points — in reference the subject already is the relation, so placing m there changes nothing; representation is the mirror on the object side; individuality is the collapsed floor. Nothing structurally new. But identification is different, and this is the case I'd never actually worked. Base x =t> x. If you tried to read it as a most-specific check — (x,x) == t — you'd force t == x, because (x,x) == x. Contradiction for any t ≠ x. So identification cannot be used to check most-specificity — the substitutions there are about t, not x:
t =t> x is t referring to x, x =t> t is x sitting in t's representation. So t is a representation that refers to x and holds x in its representation — about x without being x. That's Animal and Dog exactly: Animal refers to Dog, Dog is in Animal's representation, Animal is not Dog. t plays Animal, x plays Dog. I should have seen this on my own from the substitution, and I didn't because I hadn't done it.
And then the tower. Iterate identification — a₀ =a₁> a₀, a₁ =a₂> a₁, … — and each aₖ is a type of the level below: it refers downward and the level below sits in its representation. T-trans on -> gives you transitivity of the chain, Animal =type> Dog =type> Fido. The floor is aₙ =aₙ> aₙ — the literal individual, which the whole tower refers to and represents, but which is just an individual, nothing beneath it. Type semantics falls out as the shadow of iterated identification under the four-placement axiom. That's a real answer to "type semantics had to come from somewhere" — it comes from identification folding on itself, each level a representation-that-refers-down, bottoming out at a literal.
